title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: James wants towns to decide data center rules amid power and water battles.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're diving into a major candidate's stance on who should call the shots on these massive projects.
Right, and it's landing right in the middle of some very heated local debates.
Exactly. U.S. Senate candidate John James told The Detroit News today that he'd leave data-center siting and tax decisions to local officials rather than impose state rules.
That position feels pretty significant given what's already happening in places like Saline and Coldwater.
It does. Those townships have residents pushing back hard over power use, water draw, and tax breaks, so handing more power to locals could change how these projects move forward.
Why do you think this matters for voters heading into the August 4 primary?
Because data-center-heavy counties will be watching closely to see if this local-control approach resonates or if people want more state oversight to protect infrastructure.
And the history here goes back a bit, right? We've seen similar fights in other states where towns felt blindsided by big facilities.
Yes, and in Michigan it's playing out township by township. The stakes include higher electric bills if the grid gets strained, water resources for cooling, and how much farmland gets converted.
What happens next if more towns follow the local route James is describing?
We could see more pauses or custom rules like the one Otsego just passed, or bids like Mason County's for the state data center, all decided closer to home.
That could slow some projects but also give communities real input on noise, traffic, and taxes.
And it keeps the pressure on candidates in both parties to clarify where they stand before the primary.
Speaking of which, we saw another candidate out in Saline yesterday making the opposite case.
We'll get to that in quick hits, but first let's stay on the bigger picture of local versus state control.
How does this affect everyday residents 30 or 60 miles away from any one site?
Because power demand is regional. A big campus pulling hundreds of megawatts can push rates up for everyone on the same grid, even if your town isn't hosting it.
And water use is another shared resource issue across county lines.
Right. The Saline River discharge permit that's open for comment right now is a perfect example of how one project's needs ripple outward.
So James's position is really testing whether voters trust their own township boards to balance jobs against those impacts.
And with the primary just days away, we'll see if that message lands in the counties already dealing with proposals.
Alright, let's move to quick hits. Starting with Genesee County.
Yesterday the economic development corporation there postponed a key environmental approval for a proposed data center.
That gives Flint-area residents extra weeks to review traffic, power, and noise concerns before any vote.
Next, Otsego city council voted yesterday to ban new data centers for a full year.
Residents near potential sites now have breathing room to shape rules protecting neighborhoods from grid strain and noise.
Mason County is also in the mix, pitching itself yesterday as the home for Michigan's official state data center.
That would bring construction jobs and tax revenue to rural western Michigan, but locals would still face questions about power and land use.
Coldwater residents got their first look at plans yesterday at a joint city council and planning meeting.
They're asking the same questions about power, water, and tax breaks that are coming up in nearby townships too.
Verrus is pushing ahead on a Michigan project even as its Salem site stalls, according to reports yesterday.
Local officials are already fielding questions about power demand and tax deals, and communities are watching to see which town lands the next facility.
Abdul El-Sayed rallied yesterday at the Saline site to criticize tax breaks and grid strain from hyperscale builds.
Residents 30 minutes away could see higher electric rates if the campus pulls hundreds of megawatts without new generation.
Dowagiac neighbors have been complaining about constant high-pitched noise from an existing facility running day and night.
Those complaints are now shaping how Cass County will handle future proposals to protect sleep and property values.
A U.S. representative called yesterday for a review of Chinese robots at Hyperscale Data's Michigan site.
That raises supply-chain security questions and could affect local construction jobs or cause delays.
And the Saline data center's river discharge permit application opened for public comment this week.
Residents in Washtenaw County are watching for impacts on water quality tied to the project's operations.
Now let's look ahead to what's on deck.
Monday, August 3, the Delta County Planning Commission has a Data Center Subcommittee Update and zoning ordinance discussion on the agenda.
That's a chance for residents to weigh in on how the county might handle future proposals.
Listeners can check the county website for times and locations.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: John James Backs Local Control on Data Centers as Township Fights Intensify
